catalog_quote: Stress in Kagayanen is contrastive, and consists of lengthening of a syllable nucleus. Rise in voice pitch and intensity does not always fall on the stressed syllable, as these are high level phenomena involving intonation at the phrase or clause level. Isolated words can be pronounced with very different pitch and intensity from the same words used in communicative contexts. Because of these factors, it has been very difficult to mark words consistently for stress outside of elicitation of individual words. Stress occurs on any of the syllables of two and three syllable words. With four and five syllable words, usually there is primary stress on the penultimate and secondary stress on the second syllable to the left of the penultimate. Table 2.10 and Table 2.11 illustrate contrasting stress patterns in two and three syllable words. [p. 29, Table 2.10:] [Ɂá.naj] ‘termite’ ... [Ɂa.náj] ‘…

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically contrastive and cued by vowel/nucleus length rather than pitch or intensity. In roots of two or three syllables it can fall on any syllable (minimal pairs like [Ɂá.naj] 'termite' vs [Ɂa.náj] 'first'; three-way contrasts in 3-syllable words). In words of four or five syllables primary stress is usually on the penult with a secondary stress two syllables to its left (e.g. [kà.li.bú.tan] 'earth'). Adding a suffix or enclitic to a penult-stressed root moves stress one syllable right (so verbal suffixes keep stress on the penult), while prefixes leave root stress untouched; the future-patient nominalizer -én is stress-attracting (§3.3.6, p. 63).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated: in 4–5-syllable words secondary stress falls on the second syllable to the left of the (penultimate) primary; also marked in 3-syllable examples (e.g. [pá.Ɂa.ɡì], [kʊ̀ l.ti.báɾ]) and in derived forms like bùnakén (p. 63).
new_statements.exceptions: The 4–5-syllable penult pattern is hedged with 'usually'; some 4-syllable examples have antepenult-type placement ([kà.la.mʊ́ n.dɪŋ] is still penult, but e.g. [bà.ð̞aj-bá.ð̞aj] reduplication). The nominalizer -én shifts primary stress to the final syllable. Authors note it has been 'very difficult to mark words consistently for stress outside of elicitation of individual words' because pitch/intensity belong to phrase intonation.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, based on elicited citation forms of individual words; authors explicitly separate phrase/clause-level pitch and intensity (intonation) from word stress. Stress is not written in the standard orthography.
new_statements.identity_note: The 2024 Language Science Press grammar is by Carol J. Pebley & Thomas E. Payne (Glottolog ref 697466); Glottolog's ref 696246 ('Pebley & MacGregor 2024, Studies in Kagayanen, 745 pp., LangSci') and the earlier scan note conflate it with the 1999 SIL booklet 'Studies in Kagayanen' (Pebley & MacGregor, 115 pp.), which contains no phonology. The grammar describes Kagayanen of Cagayancillo and mainland Palawan as one language (glottocode kaga1256, ISO cgc); MacGregor 1995 mentions an unresearched dialect 'Kinagayanen' on Coron, which has no separate glottocode. No dialect-specific stress claims are made.

new_statements.quote: We recorded nine tokens of each vowel (three tokens of three words) in a stressed word-initial open syllable immediately following either a labial or alveolar stop ˈCV.CV(C) [8]. (Stress usually occurs on the penultimate syllable in Kagayanen.) One word in our corpus lacked an initial consonant. [...] All words in our data were disyllabic. — p. 846. And p. 848: We found that a closed syllable only affects the quality of /i/ (and then only in the F2 dimension), while lack of stress by itself does not appear to be an independent indicator of allophonic movement for any sound. Having said that, lack of stress in conjunction with position in the word does affect the formant values for /u/.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with, but weaker than, the catalog's existing statement from Pebley & Payne 2024 (contrastive stress; any syllable in 2–3-syllable words; penult primary in 4+-syllable words). Olson & Mielke give penult as the usual position, which fits the 2024 grammar's treatment of penultimate stress as the default (suffixes shift stress to the penult; 4+-syllable words are penult-stressed) while its 'usually' leaves room for the contrastive non-penult cases the grammar documents. It adds nothing on secondary stress or weight and provides no stress data of its own; it does not contradict the lexical/unpredictable reading, but if read alone it would suggest a penultimate default.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The paper is an acoustic vowel study, not a description of stress; its only placement statement is a one-sentence parenthetical used to justify the stimulus design: stress 'usually' falls on the penultimate syllable, so disyllabic test words have stress on the word-initial syllable. 'Usually' marks a default/tendency, not an exceptionless rule. Word stress is treated as a real phonological property (stressed vs. unstressed syllables are used as an experimental variable), and the Discussion finds that absence of stress alone does not condition vowel allophony, though unstressed word-final position raises F1 and F2 of /u/.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the hedge 'usually' implies non-penultimate stress exists but no examples or conditions are given.
new_statements.identity_note: Olson & Mielke 2007 report on a single 27-year-old female speaker whose parents are from Cagayan Island and who grew up in Puerto Princesa, Palawan; no dialect is named beyond that. Note the catalog's author order (Mielke & Olson) is reversed relative to the paper's byline (Olson & Mielke).

readall_conflicts: Mild tension only, not a contradiction. Olson & Mielke 2007 (p. 846) say stress 'usually occurs on the penultimate syllable', a passing note in an acoustic vowel study with no stress data, whereas Pebley & Payne 2024 (§2.5, pp. 28–30), the grammar the catalog already records, say stress is contrastive and can fall on any syllable of a 2–3-syllable word, with penultimate primary stress only in words of four or more syllables and after suffixation. The two are reconcilable if penult is the statistical default and contrastive non-penult stress is the marked case; the 2007 hedge 'usually' points that way. The 2024 grammar, with its minimal pairs and explicit rules, is the better-supported source and should govern the catalog entry; the 2007 remark can be logged as a 'penult is the usual position' refinement.

sources.note: Ch. 2 §2.5 'Stress' (pp. 28–30, PDF pp. 52–54): stress is contrastive, realised as nucleus lengthening (pitch/intensity are phrase-level); it falls on any syllable of 2- and 3-syllable words (minimal pairs in Tables 2.10–2.11); in 4–5-syllable words usually primary on the penult with secondary two syllables to its left; suffix/enclitic shifts stress one syllable right, prefixes do not. §3.3.6 (p. 63): future-patient nominalizer -én attracts primary stress, unlike the homophonous unstressed irrealis -en.
